title: US accuses Australia of threatening free speech as landmark online safety bill nears passage
summary: Australia's Digital Duty of Care Bill, set to pass Parliament this week with fines of up to 5% of global revenue for tech giants, has drawn a sharp rebuke from the US ambassador, who warns it will push platforms to censor lawful speech.
content:
Australia is set to pass one of the world's toughest online safety laws this week, and the United States has made clear it does not like it. The Digital Duty of Care Bill, which requires technology companies to take proactive steps to prevent foreseeable harm on their platforms, is expected to clear the Senate on Wednesday and pass the House of Representatives before Parliament rises for the year on Thursday. The legislation would expose the world's largest tech companies to fines of up to 5 per cent of their global revenue — penalties that could run into the billions of dollars.

The clash has opened a rare public rift between two of the closest allies in the world. Hours after meeting Communications Minister Anika Wells on Tuesday, the US ambassador to Australia, David Brat, warned on social media that the bill would force American platforms to censor lawful speech. "Vaguely defined 'harms,' backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech," he wrote. "As Australia's largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors."

The Trump administration had already lodged what it called "serious concerns" in a submission to a parliamentary committee in September, objecting in particular to how Australia would define "foreseeable harm." That phrase sits at the heart of the dispute: the government argues it is the only workable standard for a duty that must cover everything from scams and deepfakes to content promoting violence, while Washington and the industry argue it is too vague to build a compliance system around.

Under the bill, digital service providers — including social media platforms, games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots — would have to build safety into their products from the start rather than cleaning up harm after it happens. The government says the law sets minimum safety standards and shifts responsibility onto the companies that design the services. "We can't cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks," Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra, according to [the Straits Times](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/us-criticises-australia-social-media-law-as-harming-free-speech?ref=latest).

The bill reached the floor only after the government struck a deal with the Greens, the minor party whose support it needed in a Senate where no party holds a majority. The Greens' amendments raised the maximum penalty from A$109 million (about US$72 million) to 5 per cent of a company's global revenue and gave individuals the right to sue companies that breach the duty. Wells announced the deal on Tuesday, and the Senate was expected to pass the bill on Wednesday.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has defended the reforms, arguing they give users greater control over what they see online rather than expanding government control over speech. The government also moved to reassure critics that ordinary political debate would not be caught: amendments released on Tuesday specify that disagreeing with feminism, gender equality policies or ideas about gender roles would not, by itself, be treated as harmful content. Instead, platforms would be required to tackle material that promotes hatred of women, claims women are inherently inferior, or advocates violence, coercive control and their exclusion from public life.

That reassurance has not satisfied the opposition. The conservative Liberal Party shares Washington's concerns that the bill hands government ministers and the online safety watchdog too much power to decide what counts as harmful. "This bill undermines both the online safety of Australians and our freedom of expression," senior opposition senator Sarah Henderson told reporters. Wells, for her part, described her meeting with Brat as "useful" and said the two sides were working through their differences. "There are points of difference and we're ironing them out," she said.

Australia is not the first country to impose a duty of care on the internet, but its version goes further than most. The legislation resembles the European Union's Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and Britain's Online Safety Act, passed a year later — yet neither of those laws pairs a broad duty of care with fines of 5 per cent of global revenue. Brussels has already begun using its own powers aggressively, as shown by the European Commission's recent action against the Chinese e-commerce giant Temu under [the EU's Digital Services Act](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/eu-charges-temu-dsa-second-fine-november-2026), where a second fine is now on the table. Canberra's bill, if it works as intended, would give Australia enforcement muscle of a similar order — and, its critics say, a similar capacity to shape how global platforms behave far beyond its borders.

The dispute also fits a wider pattern. Australia has already become the first country to ban under-16s from social media, a move that drew criticism from the US and from platforms including Reddit. The duty-of-care bill extends the same logic from children to all users, and from access to the design of the services themselves. Whether other governments follow will depend in part on what happens next: if the law survives its first court challenges and the first enforcement cases, it will become a template. If it collapses into the definitional disputes Washington is warning about, it will become a cautionary tale. For now, the more immediate question is whether the argument with Washington escalates. The US is Australia's largest foreign investor and its closest security partner, and the Trump administration has shown itself willing to use tariffs and other leverage in disputes with allies. Wells said discussions were continuing. Both governments, for the moment, are still talking.
